   400	  $\{e_1,\ldots,e_t\}$ of $\F_q$ over $\F_p$ specified by
   401	  Lemma~\ref{lem:efficient_basis}.
   402	  In particular, $\downsize$ is linear over $\F_p$, and by
   403	  Lemma~\ref{lem:downsize_subspace}, the set $\downsize(V)$ is the linear space
   404	  $\F_p^{nt}$.
   405	  Define the \emph{downsized function} $L^\downsize : \downsize(V) \to
   406	  \downsize(V)$ by $L^\downsize = \downsize \circ L \circ \downsize^{-1}$.
   407	\end{definition}

+/-- Formalization-only auxiliary equivalence splitting an ambient low-degree
+vector into its point, seed, and direction blocks. -/
+private def ldSpaceSplit (L : LdParams) :
+    LdSpace L ≃ ((Fin L.m → ScalarQ L) × ScalarQ L) × (Fin L.m → ScalarQ L) where
+  toFun z := ((LdSpace.point z, LdSpace.seed z), LdSpace.direction z)
+  invFun p := fun i =>
+    match i with
+    | .inl (.inl j) => p.1.1 j
+    | .inl (.inr _) => p.1.2
+    | .inr j => p.2 j
+  left_inv z := by
+    funext i
+    rcases i with (j | u) | j
+    · rfl
+    · cases u
+      rfl
+    · rfl
+  right_inv p := by
+    obtain ⟨⟨a, b⟩, c⟩ := p
+    rfl

   675	/-- A map is `ell`-level conditionally linear exactly when it admits the

   678	theorem isCondLinear_iff_nonempty_clData {K ι : Type*} [Field K]
   679	    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] {ell : ℕ} (hEll : 1 ≤ ell)
   680	    (L : (ι → K) → (ι → K)) :
   681	    IsCondLinear ell L ↔ Nonempty (CLData K ι ell L) := by

   695	      top := d.top
   696	    }⟩
   697	  · rintro ⟨d⟩
   698	    have hPos : 0 < ell := by omega
   699	    let last : Fin ell := ⟨ell - 1, Nat.sub_lt hPos (by decide)⟩
   700	    have hLast := d.marginal_cl last
   701	    rw [d.top hPos] at hLast

   704	/-- Coordinate direct sum of maps supported on a finite register partition.
   705	This is a formalization-only auxiliary for `lem:cl-func-prod`, blueprint
   706	`ch12_qpbt_games.tex:565-576`, paper
   707	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:315-364`. -/
   708	def condLinearDirectSum {K ι : Type*} [Field K] [DecidableEq ι] {m : ℕ}
   709	    (V : Fin m → Finset ι) (L : Fin m → (ι → K) → (ι → K))
   710	    (x : ι → K) : ι → K :=
   711	  ∑ j : Fin m, L j (coordinateRestriction (V j) x)
   712	
   713	/-- Maximum of the levels in a finite direct sum. This formalization-only
   714	auxiliary uses `0` for the empty family; `lem:cl-func-prod` separately assumes
   715	the source boundary `m ≥ 1`. -/
   716	def directSumLevel {m : ℕ} (ell : Fin m → ℕ) : ℕ :=

   718

   722	`references/qpbt-paper/05_conditionally_linear_functions.tex:315-364`. -/
   723	theorem IsCondLinear.directSum {K ι : Type*} [Field K]
   724	    [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] {m : ℕ} (hm : 1 ≤ m)
   725	    (V : Fin m → Finset ι) (ell : Fin m → ℕ)
   726	    (L : Fin m → (ι → K) → (ι → K))
   727	    (hDisjoint : ∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (V i) (V j))
   728	    (hCover : ∀ a, ∃ i, a ∈ V i)
   729	    (hL : ∀ j, IsCondLinearOn K (V j) (ell j) (L j)) :
   730	    IsCondLinear (directSumLevel ell) (condLinearDirectSum V L) := by
   731	  classical
   732	  let _sourceIndex : Fin m := ⟨0, hm⟩
   733	  have hLevel (j : Fin m) : ell j ≤ directSumLevel ell :=
   734	    Finset.le_sup (f := ell) (Finset.mem_univ j)
   735	  have hRaised (j : Fin m) :
   736	      IsCondLinearOn K (V j) (directSumLevel ell) (L j) :=
   737	    IsCondLinearOn.mono_level (hL j) (hLevel j)
   738	  have hUnion : Finset.univ.biUnion V = (Finset.univ : Finset ι) := by
   739	    apply Finset.eq_univ_of_forall
   740	    intro a
   741	    obtain ⟨j, haj⟩ := hCover a
   742	    exact Finset.mem_biUnion.mpr ⟨j, Finset.mem_univ _, haj⟩
   743	  have hSum := IsCondLinearOn.directSum_sameLevel V (directSumLevel ell) L
   744	    hDisjoint hRaised
   745	  rw [hUnion] at hSum

   747	
   748	/-- Extend a vector on a register by zero to the ambient coordinate space. -/
   749	private def extendRegister {K ι : Type*} [Zero K] [DecidableEq ι]
   750	    (S : Finset ι) (x : S → K) : ι → K := fun a =>
   751	  if ha : a ∈ S then x ⟨a, ha⟩ else 0
   752	
   753	/-- A partition of the ambient coordinates identifies ambient vectors with
   754	tuples of vectors on the partition registers. -/
   755	private noncomputable def coordinatePartitionEquiv {K ι J : Type*}
   756	    [AddCommMonoid K] [Fintype ι] [DecidableEq ι] [Fintype J] [DecidableEq J]
   757	    (V : J → Finset ι) (hDisjoint : ∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (V i) (V j))
   758	    (hCover : ∀ a, ∃ j, a ∈ V j) : (ι → K) ≃ ∀ j, V j → K where
   759	  toFun x := fun _ a => x a
   760	  invFun x := ∑ j, extendRegister (V j) (x j)
   761	  left_inv x := by
   762	    funext a
   763	    obtain ⟨j, haj⟩ := hCover a
   764	    change (∑ i, extendRegister (V i) (fun b => x b)) a = x a
   765	    rw [Finset.sum_apply, Finset.sum_eq_single j]
   766	    · simp [extendRegister, haj]
   767	    · intro i _ hij
   768	      have hai : a ∉ V i := fun hai =>
   769	        Finset.disjoint_left.mp (hDisjoint i j hij) hai haj
   770	      simp [extendRegister, hai]
   771	    · exact fun hj => (hj (Finset.mem_univ j)).elim
   772	  right_inv x := by
   773	    funext j a
   774	    change (∑ i, extendRegister (V i) (x i)) a.1 = x j a
   775	    rw [Finset.sum_apply, Finset.sum_eq_single j]
   776	    · simp [extendRegister, a.2]
   777	    · intro i _ hij
   778	      have hai : a.1 ∉ V i := fun hai =>
   779	        Finset.disjoint_left.mp (hDisjoint i j hij) hai a.2
   780	      simp [extendRegister, hai]

    95	The other additional test is a ``consistency test'', where both players receive

    98	In all cases they are expected to respond with the same answer.
    99	
   100	
   101	
   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}
   175	
   176	
   177	
   178	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   179	We now present the question distribution of the game $\game^\ld$ as a typed CL
   180	distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL functions and
   181	typed CL distributions).
   182	The type set $\type^\ld$ of the game $\game^\ld$ we use is
   183	\[
   184		\type^\ld = \{ \Point, \ALine, \DLine \}\;.
   185	\]
   186	The distribution over question types is uniform over $\type^\ld \times \type^\ld$. 
   187	
   188	We introduce the corresponding typed CL functions $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$,
   189	$L_\DLine$ where the corresponding CL distributions $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$
   190	and $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$ implement the axis line-versus-point and diagonal
   210	  \label{eq:cl-alnf}
   211		L_\ALine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{e_i}(u), s, 0)\ \text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V,
   212	\end{equation}
   213	where $L^\lnf$ is the linear function used to compute the canonical
   214	representative of lines (see \Cref{def:line-representative}), and $i = \chi(s)$
   215	where we define $\chi(s)$ to be the unique integer such that
   216	\begin{equation}
   217	\label{eq:chi-func}
   218		s = (\chi(s) - 1) \frac{q}{m} + r
   219	\end{equation}
   220	for some $0 \leq r < q/m$, and we interpret the field element $s \in \F_q$ as an
   221	integer between $0$ and $q - 1$).
   222	The function $L_\ALine$ is the concatenation of the $1$-level CL function that
   223	projects the subspaces $V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ down to $V_\coord$ (i.e.
   224	zeroes out the entire $V_{\dir{}}$ register), and the family of $1$-level CL
   225	functions $\{L^\lnf_{e_i} \}$ acting on $V_\xpt$, indexed by $i \in
   226	\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   227	(See \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation.)
   228	Thus $L_\ALine$ is a $2$-level CL function.
   229	
   230	Define $L_\DLine$ to be the following $3$-level CL function: for all $(u,s,v) \in
   231	V$,
   232	\begin{equation}
   233	\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
   234		L_\DLine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),s,\pi_{i-1}(v))
   235	\end{equation}
   236	where $i = \chi(s)$.
   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.
   238	
   239	
   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}
   258	
   259	
   260	
   261	\begin{lemma}
   262		\label{lem:dlnf}
   263		Consider the pair $(\line,u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   264	  tuple $((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$,
   265	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   266	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a random
   267	  diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares the first $i-1$ coordinates
   268	  with $u$, for uniformly random $i$.
   269	\end{lemma}
   270	\begin{proof}
   271		The proof of this follows identically to \Cref{lem:alnf}.
   272	\end{proof}
   273	
   274	For later convenience we make the following definition. 
   275	
   276	\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]
   277	        \label{def:line-point-dist}
   278	 The \emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\ALine}$ is the
   279	 distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$ over pairs $(\ell=(u_0,e_i),u)$
   280	 (we omit the $0$ elements for simplicity). The \emph{diagonal
   281	   line-point distribution} $D_{\DLine}$ is the distribution
   282	 $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$  over $(\ell=(u_0,s,v),u)$. The
   283	 \emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\Line}$ is the equal mixture of the axis-parallel line-point distribution and the diagonal line-point distribution.
   284	 In other words, a sample from $D_{\Line}$ is distributed as follows:
   285	 with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\ALine}$,
   286	 and with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\DLine}$.
   287	\end{definition}
   288

   950	In the $\gamma = 1$ case, on the other hand, the measurements anticommute, which implies that they cannot simultaneously be measured.
   951	In spite of this, the verifier can still check that the measurements anticommute by using the Magic Square game from Section~\ref{sec:ms} above.
   952	As was shown in Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, any pair of anticommuting measurements
   953	can be used to form a perfect strategy for the Magic Square game
   954	(and indeed the reverse is true as well: any perfect strategy for the Magic Square game entails a pair of anticommuting measurements).

   957	
   958	\begin{definition}[Admissible parameters]\label{def:admissible}
   959	  We say that the tuple $\qldparams=(q, m, d)$ is \emph{admissible} if $q$ is
   960	  an admissible field size (Definition~\ref{def:admissible-size}) and $m | q$.

   978	
   979	Before presenting the CL functions of the Pauli basis test, we first give an

   981	pair of questions $((\tvar_\alice, x_\alice), (\tvar_\bob, x_\bob))$ in

   990		\item (\emph{Points}) $u_\xpt,u_\zpt \in \F_q^m$,
   991		\item (\emph{Directions}) $s \in \F_q$, $v \in \F_q^m$,
   992	  \item (\emph{Qubit basis for (anti-)commutation}) $r_\xpt,r_\zpt \in \F_q$.
   993		\end{enumerate}
   994	\item For $w \in \AB$ and $W\in\{X,Z\}$,
   995		\begin{enumerate}
   996	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Point, W)$, then set $x_w = u_W$,
   997	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\ALine, W)$, then set $x_w = (u_0,s)$, where $u_0 =
   998	    L^\lnf_{e_i}(u_W)$, with $i = \chi(s)$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-game} for
   999	    definition of $L^\lnf$ and $\chi(s)$),
  1000	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\DLine,W)$, then set $x_w = (u_0,s,v')$, where $i =
  1001	    \chi(s)$, $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v)$, and $u_0 = L^\lnf_{v'}(u_W)$,

  1006	  \item If $\tvar_w = \Pair$, then set $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,
  1007	  \item If $\tvar_w = (\Pair, W)$, then set $x_w = (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$,

    30	/-- Numerical parameters for the low-degree game.  The ambient coefficient
    31	space uses the once-and-for-all model `fixedFieldModel P.q P.hq`, rather than a
    32	model supplied by each parameter record.  This is the Lean carrier for
    33	`def:ld-game` in
    34	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-105`, with paper origin
    35	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
    36	-/
    37	structure LdParams where
    38	  q : ℕ
    39	  m : ℕ
    40	  d : ℕ
    41	  k : ℕ
    42	  hm : 1 ≤ m
    43	  hd : 1 ≤ d
    44	  hk : 1 ≤ k
    45	  hq : IsAdmissibleSize q
    46	  hdvd : m ∣ q
    47	
    48	/-- The positive dimension in `LdParams` supplies the finite coordinate type
    49	used by the uniform axis and prefix-index marginals. -/
    50	instance (L : LdParams) : Nonempty (Fin L.m) :=
    51	  ⟨⟨0, lt_of_lt_of_le Nat.zero_lt_one L.hm⟩⟩
    52	
    53	/-- The fixed model accessor for an `LdParams` record.  It is a compatibility
    54	view of the global `fixedFieldModel` selector, not an independently quantified
    55	parameter.  Blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`; paper origin
    56	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
    57	-/
    58	noncomputable def LdParams.model (P : LdParams) : FixedFieldModel P.q :=
    59	  fixedFieldModel P.q P.hq
    60	
    61	/-- The scalar carrier selected by an `LdParams` record; this is the fixed
    62	field carrier in `def:ld-game`, selected globally by `LdParams.model`.
    63	Blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`, paper origin
    64	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
    65	-/
    66	abbrev ScalarQ (P : LdParams) := (P.model).K
    67	
    68	/-- The three low-degree question types of `def:ld-game`, blueprint
    69	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`, paper origin
    70	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
    71	-/
    72	inductive LdType where
    73	  | point
    74	  | aline
    75	  | dline
    76	  deriving DecidableEq, Repr, Inhabited, Fintype
    77	
    78	/-- The register index used by the low-degree game (`def:ld-game`, blueprint
    79	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`; paper origin
    80	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).
    81	-/
    82	abbrev LdIndex (P : LdParams) := (Fin P.m ⊕ Unit) ⊕ Fin P.m
    83	
    84	/-- The full ambient low-degree coefficient space (`def:ld-game`, blueprint
    85	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-31`; paper origin
    86	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).
    87	-/
    88	abbrev LdSpace (P : LdParams) := LdIndex P → ScalarQ P
    89	
    90	/-- The point coordinates of an ambient low-degree vector in
    91	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
    92	-/
    93	def LdSpace.point {P : LdParams} (z : LdSpace P) : Fin P.m → ScalarQ P :=
    94	  fun i => z (.inl (.inl i))
    95	
    96	/-- The shared scalar coordinate of an ambient low-degree vector in
    97	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
    98	-/
    99	def LdSpace.seed {P : LdParams} (z : LdSpace P) : ScalarQ P :=
   100	  z (.inl (.inr ()) )
   101	
   102	/-- The direction coordinates of an ambient low-degree vector in
   103	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   104	-/
   105	def LdSpace.direction {P : LdParams} (z : LdSpace P) : Fin P.m → ScalarQ P :=
   106	  fun i => z (.inr i)
   107	
   108	/-- The integer-coordinate map `χ` from the fixed field representation.  This
   109	is `eq:chi-func` in `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
   110	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
   111	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   112	-/
   113	noncomputable def chiIndex (P : LdParams) (s : ScalarQ P) : Fin P.m := by
   114	  letI : NeZero P.m := ⟨by
   115	    exact Nat.ne_of_gt (lt_of_lt_of_le Nat.zero_lt_one P.hm)⟩
   116	  exact Fin.ofNat P.m ((binaryRepresentation P.model s).val / (P.q / P.m))
   117	
   118	/-- The projection used in the diagonal-line map zeroes coordinates before the
   119	chosen index and retains the suffix of the direction vector.  This is the
   120	prefix restriction in `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
   121	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
   122	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   123	-/
   124	def prefixProjection {P : LdParams} (i : Fin P.m) (v : Fin P.m → ScalarQ P) :
   125	    Fin P.m → ScalarQ P :=
   126	  fun j => if j.val < i.val then 0 else v j
   127	
   128	/-- The point CL map, retaining the point block and clearing the auxiliary
   129	blocks.  It is the map `L_point` of `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
   130	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
   131	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   132	-/
   133	def ldPointCL (P : LdParams) (z : LdSpace P) : LdSpace P :=
   134	  fun i => match i with
   135	  | .inl (.inl j) => z (.inl (.inl j))
   136	  | .inl (.inr _) => 0
   137	  | .inr _ => 0
   138	
   139	/-- The affine-line CL map.  The direction block is put through the canonical
   140	line representative map from `def:line-representative`, while the point block
   141	is retained (blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`; paper
   142	origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).
   143	-/
   144	noncomputable def ldALineCL (P : LdParams) (z : LdSpace P) : LdSpace P :=
   145	  let i := chiIndex P (z.seed)
   146	  let rep := lineRepMap (coordinateDirection i)
   147	  fun i => match i with
   148	  | .inl (.inl j) => (rep (z.point)) j
   149	  | .inl (.inr _) => z (.inl (.inr ()))
   150	  | .inr _ => 0
   151	
   152	/-- The diagonal-line CL map, using the same canonical representative interface
   153	for the direction block.  This is the `L_DLine` clause of
   154	`def:ld-question-distribution` (blueprint
   155	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`; paper origin
   156	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`).
   157	-/
   158	noncomputable def ldDLineCL (P : LdParams) (z : LdSpace P) : LdSpace P :=
   159	  let i := chiIndex P (z.seed)
   160	  let direction := prefixProjection i (z.direction)
   161	  let rep := lineRepMap direction
   162	  fun i => match i with
   163	  | .inl (.inl j) => (rep (z.point)) j
   164	  | .inl (.inr _) => z (.inl (.inr ()))
   165	  | .inr j => direction j
   166	
   167	/-- Dispatch the three low-degree CL maps by question type.  This is the typed
   168	construction in `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
   169	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
   170	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   171	-/
   172	noncomputable def ldCL (P : LdParams) : LdType → LdSpace P → LdSpace P
   173	  | .point => ldPointCL P
   174	  | .aline => ldALineCL P
   175	  | .dline => ldDLineCL P

   374	private noncomputable def ldDLineTerm (P : LdParams) :
   375	    CondLinearTerm (ScalarQ P) (ι := LdIndex P) 3 :=

   387	/-- The conditional-linearity level of the affine-line map.  This is a named
   388	Lean proof obligation for the prose assertion in `def:ld-question-distribution`,
   389	blueprint `blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper

   391	-/
   392	theorem isCondLinear_ldALineCL (P : LdParams) :
   393	    IsCondLinearOn (ScalarQ P) Finset.univ 2 (ldALineCL P) := by
   394	  refine ⟨ldALineTerm P, ⟨Finset.subset_univ _, fun _ =>
   395	    ⟨ldPointRegister_subset_sdiff_seed P, fun _ => trivial⟩⟩, ?_⟩
   396	  funext x
   397	  have hseed :
   398	      LdSpace.seed (ldSeedLinear P (coordinateRestriction (ldSeedRegister P) x)) =
   399	        LdSpace.seed x := coordinateRestriction_seed P x
   400	  have hpoint : LdSpace.point (coordinateRestriction (ldPointRegister P) x) =
   401	      LdSpace.point x := coordinateRestriction_point P x
   402	  have hval :
   403	      CondLinearTerm.eval (ldALineTerm P) x =
   404	        ldSeedLinear P (coordinateRestriction (ldSeedRegister P) x) +
   405	          (ldPointCLLinear P (coordinateDirection (chiIndex P (LdSpace.seed x)))
   406	            (coordinateRestriction (ldPointRegister P) x) + 0) := by
   407	    change ldSeedLinear P (coordinateRestriction (ldSeedRegister P) x) +
   408	        (ldPointCLLinear P
   409	            (coordinateDirection (chiIndex P
   410	              (LdSpace.seed (ldSeedLinear P (coordinateRestriction (ldSeedRegister P) x)))))
   411	            (coordinateRestriction (ldPointRegister P) x) + 0) = _
   412	    rw [hseed]
   413	  rw [hval]
   414	  funext i
   415	  rcases i with (j | u) | j
   416	  · change (0 : ScalarQ P) +
   417	        (lineRepMap (coordinateDirection (chiIndex P (LdSpace.seed x)))
   418	          (LdSpace.point (coordinateRestriction (ldPointRegister P) x)) j + 0) =
   419	      lineRepMap (coordinateDirection (chiIndex P (LdSpace.seed x)))
   420	        (LdSpace.point x) j
   421	    rw [hpoint, zero_add, add_zero]
   422	  · change coordinateRestriction (ldSeedRegister P) x (Sum.inl (Sum.inr ())) +
   423	        ((0 : ScalarQ P) + 0) = x (Sum.inl (Sum.inr ()))
   424	    rw [coordinateRestriction_seed, add_zero, add_zero]
   425	  · change (0 : ScalarQ P) + ((0 : ScalarQ P) + 0) = 0
   426	    rw [add_zero, add_zero]
   427	
   428	/-- The conditional-linearity level of the diagonal-line map.  This is the
   429	level-3 assertion in `def:ld-question-distribution`, blueprint
   430	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:38-49`, paper origin
   431	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.

   433	theorem isCondLinear_ldDLineCL (P : LdParams) :
   434	    IsCondLinearOn (ScalarQ P) Finset.univ 3 (ldDLineCL P) := by
   435	  refine ⟨ldDLineTerm P, ⟨Finset.subset_univ _, fun _ =>
   436	    ⟨ldDirectionRegister_subset_sdiff_seed P, fun _ =>
   437	      ⟨ldPointRegister_subset_sdiff_seed_direction P, fun _ => trivial⟩⟩⟩, ?_⟩
   438	  funext x
   439	  have hseed :
   440	      LdSpace.seed (ldSeedLinear P (coordinateRestriction (ldSeedRegister P) x)) =
   441	        LdSpace.seed x := coordinateRestriction_seed P x

   443	      LdSpace.point x := coordinateRestriction_point P x
   444	  have hdir :
   445	      LdSpace.direction
   446	          (ldDirectionCLLinear P (chiIndex P (LdSpace.seed x))

   449	    funext j

   454	      CondLinearTerm.eval (ldDLineTerm P) x =
   455	        ldSeedLinear P (coordinateRestriction (ldSeedRegister P) x) +
   456	          (ldDirectionCLLinear P (chiIndex P (LdSpace.seed x))
   457	              (coordinateRestriction (ldDirectionRegister P) x) +
   458	            (ldPointCLLinear P
   459	                (prefixProjection (chiIndex P (LdSpace.seed x)) (LdSpace.direction x))
   460	                (coordinateRestriction (ldPointRegister P) x) + 0)) := by
   461	    change ldSeedLinear P (coordinateRestriction (ldSeedRegister P) x) +
   462	        (ldDirectionCLLinear P
   463	            (chiIndex P
   464	              (LdSpace.seed (ldSeedLinear P (coordinateRestriction (ldSeedRegister P) x))))

   466	          (ldPointCLLinear P
   467	              (LdSpace.direction
   468	                (ldDirectionCLLinear P
   469	                  (chiIndex P
   470	                    (LdSpace.seed
   471	                      (ldSeedLinear P (coordinateRestriction (ldSeedRegister P) x))))
   472	                  (coordinateRestriction (ldDirectionRegister P) x)))
   473	              (coordinateRestriction (ldPointRegister P) x) + 0)) = _
   474	    rw [hseed, hdir]
   475	  rw [hval]
   476	  funext i
   477	  rcases i with (j | u) | j
   478	  · change (0 : ScalarQ P) + ((0 : ScalarQ P) +
   479	        (lineRepMap
   480	          (prefixProjection (chiIndex P (LdSpace.seed x)) (LdSpace.direction x))
   481	          (LdSpace.point (coordinateRestriction (ldPointRegister P) x)) j + 0)) =
   482	      lineRepMap (prefixProjection (chiIndex P (LdSpace.seed x)) (LdSpace.direction x))
   483	        (LdSpace.point x) j
   484	    rw [hpoint, zero_add, zero_add, add_zero]
   485	  · change coordinateRestriction (ldSeedRegister P) x (Sum.inl (Sum.inr ())) +
   590	def alinePointCondition (P : LdParams) (line point : LdSpace P)
   591	    (f : Fin P.k → Fin (P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
   592	    (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P) : Prop :=
   593	  -- Universal quantification follows the zero-direction convention in
   594	  -- `rem:ld-win-zero-direction`.
   595	  ∀ t : ScalarQ P,
   596	    point.point = line.point + t • coordinateDirection (chiIndex P line.seed) →
   597	      ∀ j : Fin P.k, evalCoefficient (f j) t = a j
   598	
   599	/-- The diagonal line/point relation in `def:ld-win-predicate`, blueprint
   600	`ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   601	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   602	-/
   603	def dlinePointCondition (P : LdParams) (line point : LdSpace P)
   604	    (f : Fin P.k → Fin (P.m * P.d + 1) → ScalarQ P)
   605	    (a : Fin P.k → ScalarQ P) : Prop :=
   606	  ∀ t : ScalarQ P,
   607	    point.point = line.point + t • line.direction →
   608	      ∀ j : Fin P.k, evalCoefficient (f j) t = a j
   609	
   610	/-- The low-degree consistency predicate, rejecting answers of the wrong
   611	constructor shape.  This is `def:ld-win-predicate` in
   612	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:56-105`, paper origin
   613	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   614	-/
   615	noncomputable def ldWinPredicate (P : LdParams) :
   616	    LdQuestion P → LdQuestion P → LdAnswer P → LdAnswer P → Bool :=
   617	  open Classical in
   618	  fun (tA, xA) (tB, xB) a b =>
   619	      if validLdAnswer tA a && validLdAnswer tB b then
   620	        match tA, tB, a, b with
   621	        | .point, .point, .pointVals u, .pointVals v => decide (u = v)
   622	        | .aline, .point, .alinePolys f, .pointVals u =>
   623	            decide (alinePointCondition P xA xB f u)
   624	        | .point, .aline, .pointVals u, .alinePolys f =>
   625	            decide (alinePointCondition P xB xA f u)
   626	        | .dline, .point, .dlinePolys f, .pointVals u =>
   627	            decide (dlinePointCondition P xA xB f u)
   628	        | .point, .dline, .pointVals u, .dlinePolys f =>
   629	            decide (dlinePointCondition P xB xA f u)
   630	        | .aline, .aline, .alinePolys f, .alinePolys g => decide (f = g)
   631	        | .dline, .dline, .dlinePolys f, .dlinePolys g => decide (f = g)
   632	        | _, _, _, _ => true
   633	      else false
   634	
   635	/-- The low-degree game packaged as a `Game`.  This is `def:ld-game` in
   636	`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:17-105`, paper origin
   637	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:31-391`.
   638	-/
   639	noncomputable def ldGame (P : LdParams) : Game where
   640	  QuestionA := LdQuestion P
   641	  QuestionB := LdQuestion P
   642	  AnswerA := LdAnswer P
   643	  AnswerB := LdAnswer P
   644	  μ := ldQuestionDistribution P
   645	  μ_prob := by
   646	    exact Distribution.IsProbability.map
   647	      (uniformDistribution_isProbability ((LdType × LdType) × LdSpace P)) _
   648	  decide := ldWinPredicate P
   649	
   650	end

1	# Blueprint Style Guide & Lessons Learned
     2	
     3	## Core Philosophy
     4	The blueprint is a **bridge between the mathematics and the Lean formalization**. A reader should be able to read a blueprint entry and immediately understand the corresponding Lean declaration. Conversely, someone reading the Lean code should find the blueprint proof sketch faithful to what the code actually does.
     5	
     6	## General Principles
     7	1. **Blueprint ↔ Lean must match.** Every `\lean{X}` tag must correspond to an actual Lean declaration. Every proof sketch must match what the Lean proof actually does — not a hand-wavy version of it.
     8	2. **Standalone.** `blueprint/` and any slides are independent — no cross-references, no shared files. Each has its own macros, its own `references.bib`.
     9	3. **Mathematical language only — zero Lean jargon.** No Lean identifiers in prose (no `selfImprovement_step`, no `PastingLemma.aux`, no `rintro ⟨X, hX⟩`). The `\lean{...}` tag is the link; the body text is standard mathematics. If you can't say it in math, rewrite it.
    10	4. **No filler prose.** Only precise definitions, theorem statements, and proof sketches. No "this is important because..." or "the self-improvement step governs the induction...".
    11	5. **Cite non-trivial things.** Basic definitions don't need citations. Important results and non-obvious definitions should cite the source paper.
    12	6. **Don't invent terminology or notation.** Don't create ad-hoc notation when standard notation exists. Don't name things that the literature doesn't name.
    13	7. **Match Lean's theorem/lemma/def exactly.** If Lean says `theorem X`, use `\begin{theorem}`. If Lean says `lemma X`, use `\begin{lemma}`. `\begin{proposition}` is allowed in blueprint prose when it improves mathematical readability, but still map it to an actual Lean `theorem`/`lemma` declaration via `\lean{...}`. Label prefix: `thm:` for theorem, `lem:` for lemma, `def:` for definition, `prop:` for proposition.
    14	
    15	### Remark On Mathematical Prose
    16	
    17	Blueprint entries should read as mathematical exposition, not as progress
    18	reports. The mathematical argument should determine the order of the prose:
    19	introduce the notation, state the assertion, give the proof or calculation, and
    20	then record Lean references through the usual blueprint tags. Lean declarations,
    21	file paths, and proof-status information should not become the visible structure
    22	of the paragraph. When referring to a source article, cite it bibliographically
    23	rather than relying on an uncited reference to the article.
    24	
    25	Use displayed formulae when the formula benefits from visual separation, and
    26	keep short scalar definitions or elementary inequalities inline when the
    27	sentence reads better that way. As in ordinary mathematical writing, displayed
    28	formulae should be punctuated as part of the sentences in which they occur.
    29	
    30	## Proof Sketches Must Match Lean
    31	This is the most important rule. Every proof in the blueprint must faithfully describe what the Lean proof does:
    32	
    33	- **Reference the actual lemmas used.** If the Lean proof calls `LDT.selfImprovement`, the blueprint proof should say "By Lemma X.Y (self-improvement)..." and list it in `\uses`.
    34	- **Do not use `\cref` or `\Cref`.** The blueprint does not load `cleveref`.
    35	  Spell out the kind of object and use ordinary references, for example
    36	  `Lemma~\ref{lem:self-improvement}` or `Theorem~\ref{thm:main-formal}`.
    37	- **Describe the actual proof structure.** If Lean does induction on a parameter, say so. If Lean uses a specific decomposition, name it.
    38	- **Don't hand-wave where Lean is specific.** "Standard argument" is not acceptable if Lean uses three specific lemmas. Name them.
    39	- **Don't be more specific than Lean.** If Lean uses `simp` to close a goal, a one-line sketch is fine.
    40	- **`\uses` in proofs must be accurate.** Only list what the proof actually uses, not what the statement mentions.
    41	
    42	## Source-Labelled Statements And Conditional Helpers
    43	
    44	If a blueprint theorem, lemma, or proposition carries a source label from the
    45	paper, the linked Lean declaration must state the same theorem, up to faithful
    46	formal encoding of the paper's domain.  Do not use `\lean{...}` and `\leanok`
    47	on the source-labelled statement to point to a conditional helper whose
    48	additional assumptions supply an unproved part of the paper proof.
    49	Changing the Lean statement away from `references/ldt-paper/` is strongly
    50	discouraged unless faithful formal encoding or a documented mathematical
    51	necessity requires it; the blueprint should make any such necessity explicit.
    52	
    53	Boundary hypotheses such as nonemptiness, decidability, field-model instances,
    54	positivity of parameters, and denominator nonvanishing may be faithful when
    55	they express the mathematical domain that the paper leaves implicit.  By
    56	contrast, bridge inputs, residual data, repair hypotheses, producer
    57	assumptions, proof-obligation inputs, or package assumptions are proof debt.
    58	They must not be added to a source-labelled theorem statement.  If such data is
    59	still unproved, the source-labelled Lean theorem should keep the source-shaped
    60	statement and carry a tracked `sorry`, or the missing assertion should appear
    61	as the lowest named internal obligation with a tracked `sorry`.  A separately
    62	named conditional helper should not be introduced as a repair pattern.  If one
    63	already contains substantial proof content, it may remain temporarily only as
    64	quarantine: it needs a paper source, a tracking issue, and a discharge or
    65	deletion plan.  The blueprint should leave the paper theorem unmarked as
    66	proof-complete until the source-faithful Lean statement has a source-faithful
    67	proof.
    68	
    69	If a Lean theorem proves only a restricted version of a source theorem, the
    70	blueprint entry carrying `\leanok` must state that restriction in the theorem
    71	statement itself.  It must not be cited as the unrestricted source theorem.
    72	When the only Lean declaration available for a source label has extra
    73	non-paper assumptions, remove the `\leanok` claim from the source-labelled
    74	entry or move the restricted statement to a separate Lean-only entry.  The
    75	unrestricted paper theorem remains unformalized until a Lean statement with
    76	the source's hypothesis set exists.
    77	
    78	## Notation Consistency
    79	Notation must be **internally consistent** across the entire blueprint and **close to what the Lean code expresses**:
    80	
    81	- **Indices**: 0-indexed where matching `Fin n` in Lean
    82	- **Finite fields / alphabets**: use standard notation for the alphabet $\Sigma$ and finite fields $\mathbb{F}_q$
    83	- **Measurements**: use standard quantum measurement notation (projective measurements, POVMs)
    84	- **Strategies**: quantum strategies for nonlocal games should use standard notation from the literature
    85	- **Expansion**: use standard notation for graph expansion parameters
    86	- **Macros** (in `macros/common.tex`): define project-specific macros and use them consistently
    87	
    88	The original reference controls notation whenever it gives a usable convention.
    89	If the blueprint needs a different symbol, index convention, or name in order to
    90	match Lean, introduce it explicitly and relate it to the paper notation in the
    91	same paragraph.  Do not let a `\lean{...}` tag, a Lean namespace, or a file name
    92	be the only explanation of a changed term.
    93	
    94	When a public Lean declaration is a formalization-only auxiliary lemma, the
    95	blueprint should say so before listing the declaration.  The surrounding prose
    96	should identify the paper theorem, equation, or construction that the auxiliary
    97	lemma supports, and should avoid making the auxiliary name look like a named
    98	result from the source article.
    99	
   100	## What NOT to Put in the Blueprint
   101	- **Lean identifier names in math text.** Write "the self-improvement lemma", never "the `selfImprovement` step". The `\lean{LDT.selfImprovement}` tag handles the linking.
   102	- **Implementation details.** Don't say "bundled as an element of the Euclidean space" or "using `EuclideanSpace.equiv`". Describe the mathematical object.
   103	- **Ad-hoc notation.** Don't invent superscripts or subscripts to distinguish from existing notation. Use standard conventions.
   104	- **Function-call syntax.** Use mathematical notation, not programming notation.
   105	- **Redundant definitions.** If two blueprint definitions describe the same mathematical object, consolidate them. Each definition should introduce genuinely new mathematical content.
   106	- **Lean namespace prefixes in prose.** Don't write "the `LDT.PastingLemma`" — write "the pasting lemma".
   107	
   108	## Banned AI/Software Language (enforced in both blueprint AND Lean code)
   109	The blueprint reads as a **mathematical document**, not software documentation. The following patterns are banned in ALL reader-facing text (section titles, theorem names, proof sketches, remarks, chapter preambles) and in ALL Lean docstrings, comments, and section names:
   110	
   111	### Banned terms → replacements:
   112	| Banned | Use instead |
   113	|--------|------------|
   114	| "Assembly" (as section/chapter title) | "Proof of [theorem]", "Construction", "Composition" |
   115	| "Pipeline" | "reduction", "construction", "proof chain" |
   116	| "Bridge" (as noun for a connection) | "connection", name by mathematical content |
   117	| "Handoff" / "hand off" | "transition", "continuation", or drop entirely |
   118	| "In this blueprint" / "Within this blueprint" | "here", "in what follows", or omit |
   119	| "Honest" (as adjective for rigorous) | "exact", "faithful", "unconditional", "complete" |
   120	| "Glue layer" | "intermediate construction", "connecting results" |
   121	| "Re-export" / "reexport" | "provides", "re-states" |
   122	| "Wiring" / "wire up" | "connecting", "composing", "combining" |
   123	| "Package" (as noun for a data bundle) | "form", "data", "structure" |
   124	| "Sorry-free" | acceptable only in Lean-specific technical context |
   125	
   126	### Additional rules:
   127	- **Section names in Lean**: use mathematical terms (`section QuantumSoundness`, `section SelfImprovement`, `section PastingLemma`), not organizational terms (`section Assembly`, `section Pipeline`).
   128	- **Internal LaTeX labels** (e.g., `\label{ch:soundness}`) are not reader-facing and need not be renamed if doing so would break cross-references. But NEW labels should follow the standard.
   129	- **Definitions that are actually theorems**: if a statement asserts a mathematical fact, it must be `\begin{theorem}`, not `\begin{definition}`. Definitions introduce new objects; theorems prove properties.
   130	
   131	## `\uses` Dependency Guidelines
   132	- **Statement `\uses`**: list only what's needed to *state* the result (typically definitions of the objects involved). Keep minimal — transitive deps are automatic.
   133	- **Proof `\uses`**: list only what the proof *actually calls*. Don't list definitions unless the proof unfolds that definition.
   134	- **Never self-reference**: a proof's `\uses` must NOT include the label of the theorem it proves.
   135	
   136	## Recording Formalization-Only Lemmas
   137	Some Lean lemmas are genuine proof infrastructure rather than named statements
   138	from the original papers. These must be traceable without making the blueprint
   139	look as if the paper stated them.
   140	
   141	- If a declaration directly formalizes a paper or blueprint statement, record
   142	  it as usual with `\lean{...}` on that statement and cite the relevant source.
   143	- If a public declaration is an auxiliary lemma introduced only for the Lean
   144	  proof, make that status explicit. Its Lean docstring should say that it is a
   145	  formalization-only auxiliary lemma and should name the nearby paper equation,
   146	  line range, or blueprint result it supports.
   147	- If such an auxiliary declaration is important enough to be referenced from
   148	  the blueprint, give it a clearly subordinate blueprint node, for example
   149	  `[Formalization support for ...]`, and state in the first sentence that the
   150	  lemma is not a named statement of the paper but isolates a step used in the
   151	  Lean proof.
   152	- Connect auxiliary nodes to the corresponding result from the paper with `\uses{...}` from
   153	  the proof that actually calls them. Do not add them only to silence a sync
   154	  warning; the dependency edge should explain where the auxiliary result is
   155	  used.
   156	- Do not mark an auxiliary node with proof-level `\leanok` unless its Lean proof
   157	  is complete and `#print axioms` has no `sorryAx`. Statement-level `\leanok`
   158	  is acceptable only when the Lean statement is intentionally recorded but the
   159	  proof remains tracked as incomplete.
   160	
   161	## Blueprint Structure
   162	- `content.tex` is a router: `\input{chapter/ch01_intro}` etc.
   163	- Each chapter is a separate file in `chapter/`
   164	- Definitions/theorems numbered within chapters: `\newtheorem{theorem}{Theorem}[chapter]`
   165	
   166	## Lean Blueprint Macros
   167	- `\lean{Namespace.DeclName}` — links to Lean declaration
   168	- `\leanok` — context-sensitive marker; see "Statement-level vs proof-level `\leanok`" below
   169	- `\uses{label1, label2}` — declares dependency edges for the graph
   170	- `\notready` — marks as not ready for formalization (orange in graph)
   171	- `\mathlibok` — already in Mathlib (dark green in graph; see legend note below)
   172	
   173	### Statement-level vs proof-level `\leanok`
   174	
   175	`\leanok` is context-sensitive for human review and graph interpretation. The same macro is used for two different claims, so reviewers should read it by placement rather than by raw token count.
   176	
   177	**Statement-level `\leanok`.** Place this inside a `theorem`, `lemma`, `proposition`, `corollary`, or `definition` environment, on its own line immediately after `\lean{...}`. It says that the corresponding Lean declaration exists and that its statement matches the blueprint or paper statement. It does **not** say that the Lean proof already exists or is complete. For definitions, this is the only `\leanok` marker.

# Mathematical Language Guidelines

MIPStarRE Lean names and documentation should be written for readers comparing
the formalization with the paper and blueprint.

This is a project-local supplement to the Mathlib-derived documentation,
naming, and style guides in the lean-conventions skill's `MATHLIB_doc`,
`MATHLIB_naming`, and `MATHLIB_style` references.

## Scope

These guidelines apply to:

- public Lean declaration names and namespace names;
- module docstrings;
- declaration docstrings;
- documentation-visible section comments;
- explanatory comments that describe the mathematical role of a declaration.
- blueprint prose and formalization-support notes;
- issue titles and issue bodies;
- PR titles and PR descriptions.

## Source of Truth

Use terminology from the following sources, in this order:

1. `references/ldt-paper/`
2. `blueprint/src/chapter/`
3. established local conventions in nearby Lean files

When the paper has a term for the object, use that term. For Section 5, for
example, prefer orthogonalization lemma, truncation function, rounding to
projectors, rank reduction, and completing to measurement.

## Reference Notation And Terminology

The notation and terminology of the original reference are the default for
reader-facing mathematical text.  A reader should be able to compare a Lean
docstring, blueprint paragraph, issue, or PR description with the cited source
without first learning a private vocabulary used by the formalization.

When Lean must use a different name or representation, define the deviation in a
location which future readers can find from the affected statement.  Use the
first applicable location in the following order:

1. the declaration docstring of the public object whose name or representation
   differs from the paper;
2. the module docstring of the defining Lean file, when the deviation concerns a
   family of declarations in that file;
3. the relevant blueprint paragraph, when the notation appears only in the
   blueprint;
4. a report under `docs/reports/` or `docs/paper-gaps/`, when the deviation is a
   larger discrepancy between the paper, blueprint, and Lean.

The explanation should say:

- the notation or term used in the paper;
- the Lean object or name which represents it;
- the mathematical reason for the difference, if there is one;
- the scope in which the replacement should be used.

A PR description may mention the deviation, but it should not be the only place
where future readers can learn it.

Formalization-only auxiliary lemmas should be introduced as such.  Their prose
should name the nearby paper equation, theorem, or construction they support,
rather than presenting the auxiliary name as paper terminology.

## Naming Norm

Names and prose should describe the mathematical object, hypothesis, or
conclusion. They should not encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled.

Avoid presenting words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`, `raw`,
`oneShot`, or `liveBlock` as mathematical terminology unless the cited source
uses them with that meaning. Likewise, avoid implementation-local substitutes
such as `projectivization` or `spectral truncation` when the paper gives a
clearer phrase.

This is a general rule for the repository, not only a rule for file splits.
Module names, namespace names, public declarations, theorem fields, docstrings,
blueprint-facing names, issue titles, and spec documents should name the
mathematical layer under discussion, not the local workflow step, paper line
number, or implementation history.

### Concrete examples

The table below illustrates the naming norm with examples patterned on the
codebase and on names seen during review.  Some entries are existing names;
others are proposed names for future refactors.  The "avoid" column lists
process-shaped names that encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled; the "prefer" column lists mathematical names that a reader of the
paper or blueprint would recognize.

| Avoid (process-shaped)                        | Prefer (mathematical)                     | Rationale                                              |
|:----------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|
| `Line130`                                     | `ProjectiveConsistency`                   | Paper Lemma 5.13, not "the line-130 identity"          |
| `Line169`                                     | `CompletionTransport`                     | Paper Lemma 5.16, step that transports completed data  |
| `Step6`                                       | `Orthonormalization`                      | Paper Section 5, the orthonormalization construction   |
| `FinalAssembly`                               | `DiagonalCompletion`                      | Paper Lemma 5.17, constructing a diagonal POVM         |
| `OneShotIneq`                                 | `SelfConsistencyDataProcessing` (or existing module `Preliminaries.SelfConsistency.DataProcessing`)           | Paper's data-processing inequality for self-consistency |
| `PipelineCheck`                               | `ErrorPropagationBound` (proposed)                   | The bound that propagates error through the test       |
| `QxpLayerWrapper`                             | `ProjectivePOVMCompletion` (proposed)                | The construction from round-projectors to POVMs        |
| `RawSpectralTruncation`                       | `SpectralTruncation`                      | The paper's spectral truncation, not an "unwrapped" version |
| `AddInUStep3To5`                              | `AddInUUpperExcessMass` (proposed)                  | Paper Addendum in §U, the upper excess-mass estimate   |
| `AddInUStep12`                                | `AddInUCommutationTail` (proposed)                   | Paper Addendum in §U, the commutation tail estimate    |

An avoided name is acceptable only when the cited paper itself uses that
phrase as the mathematical name (e.g., a lemma the paper calls "Step 2").
In that case the docstring should cite the paper's phrasing.

File-split PRs are a common place where this rule matters: new leaves should be
named by the mathematical boundary they isolate, and any public declarations
exposed by the split should be reviewed under the same standard.

### Shared helpers

When the same (or nearly the same) helper declaration appears in two or
more chapter-local leaves, the copies should be consolidated into a single
shared helper in an appropriate common module.  This avoids duplication and
ensures that fixes, generalizations, or upstream replacements apply to all
call sites at once.  Issue [#1145] tracks this work across the repository.

Procedure:

1. **Confirm equivalence.**  Compare the statement of each copy.  If the
   types differ only by a chapter-specific parameterization (e.g.,
   `SubMeas (Polynomial params) ι` vs `SubMeas (Point params) ι`),
   parameterize the shared helper over that type via a `variable` or
   explicit argument.
2. **Find the right home.**  Prefer a module that is already imported by
   both call sites.  Typical candidates:
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Basic/` for parameter-free operators and bounds,
   - `MIPStarRE/LDT/Preliminaries/` for polynomial/field/character lemmas,
   - The highest chapter that is a common dependency of the two sites.
3. **Name mathematically.**  Give the shared helper a name that describes
   what it states, not which chapter it originally came from.
4. **Replace call sites.**  Delete the chapter-local copies and replace
   their uses with the shared helper.  A thin wrapper is allowed only when it
   preserves a paper-facing or blueprint-facing name that external readers
   need to search for; such wrappers should have a docstring or compatibility
   comment explaining why the alias exists.  Remove the wrapper once that
   paper-facing name is no longer needed for external reference.
5. **Document.**  Add a docstring to the shared helper citing the paper or
   blueprint location it supports.

### Legacy identifier treatment

If a docstring must mention a legacy Lean identifier, cite it in backticks and
describe the mathematical object in paper terminology. If an old public
identifier cannot be renamed in the current PR, record the required migration
in the issue, PR description, or an audit file under `audits/`.

Do not add an empty pass-through abbreviation merely to introduce a second
public name.  This is different from a documented public wrapper allowed in the
shared-helper procedure above: a wrapper must preserve a paper-facing or
blueprint-facing term and must say why the alias exists.

## Review Checklist

Reviewers should use this checklist when examining public names and
documentation prose.  Flag any item that fails.

- [ ] **Naming.**  Do public declaration names, namespace names, module names,
      theorem field names, and docstring prose describe a mathematical object,
      hypothesis, or conclusion?  Or do they encode the history of how the
      formalization was assembled (paper line numbers, workflow steps,
      implementation-phase labels)?
- [ ] **Source alignment.**  For the mathematical content under review, does
      the prose use the terminology in `references/ldt-paper/` or the
      blueprint?  Are process words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`,
      `raw`, `oneShot`, or `liveBlock` used as mathematical terms when the
      source does not use them that way?
- [ ] **Deviation documented.**  If a Lean name or representation differs from
      the paper, is the deviation documented in a declaration docstring,
      module docstring, blueprint paragraph, or `docs/paper-gaps/` note, in
      that order of preference?
- [ ] **Auxiliary lemmas.**  Are formalization-only auxiliary lemmas introduced
      as such, with prose naming the nearby paper equation, theorem, or
      construction they support?
- [ ] **Shared helpers.**  Does the PR introduce a helper that already exists
      (or near-exists) in another chapter-local leaf?  If so, has it been
      consolidated into a common module with a mathematical name?
- [ ] **Legacy IDs.**  If a legacy Lean identifier is mentioned, is the
      mathematical object described in paper terminology?  If an old public
      identifier cannot be renamed yet, is the required migration recorded in
      the issue, PR description, or an audit file?
- [ ] **Pass-through names.**  Does the PR add an empty pass-through
      abbreviation that introduces a second public name without adding
      mathematical content?  Reject it unless it is a documented compatibility
      wrapper preserving paper-facing or blueprint-facing terminology.

Review-fix PRs touching a surface covered by an active audit should read the
relevant audit before changing names or prose.

     5	/-!
     6	# Distribution infrastructure for the low individual degree test
     7	
     8	Shared distribution definitions: finite-support weighted distributions,
     9	a probability predicate, push-forward distributions, weighted-sum linear maps,
    10	averaging, uniform distribution, and outcome summation.
    11	
    12	Note: this module contributes declarations to the comparator statement closure
    13	of `mainFormal`, which must elaborate in the same environment as the
    14	Mathlib-only `Challenge.lean`.  Keep the full `import Mathlib`; do not narrow
    15	it.  See `docs/comparator.md`, "Environment alignment".
    16	-/
    17	
    18	open scoped BigOperators MatrixOrder Matrix ComplexOrder
    19	
    20	namespace MIPStarRE.LDT
    21	
    22	/-- A finite-support weighted distribution with nonnegative real-valued weights. -/
    23	structure Distribution (α : Type*) where
    24	  support : Finset α := ∅
    25	  weight : α → Error := fun _ => 0
    26	  nonnegative : ∀ a, 0 ≤ weight a := by intro _; positivity
    27	  outsideSupport : ∀ a, a ∉ support → weight a = 0 := by intro _ _; rfl
    28	
    29	namespace Distribution
    30	
    31	/-- The total mass carried by the explicit support of a distribution. -/
    32	def totalWeight {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) : Error :=
    33	  ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a
    34	
    35	/-- A `Distribution` is probabilistic when its total mass is exactly `1`. -/
    36	def IsProbability {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α) : Prop :=
    37	  𝒟.totalWeight = 1
    38	
    39	/-- Push a finite-support distribution forward along a map.
    40	
    41	This is the project `Distribution` analogue of `PMF.map`.  The support is the
    42	image of the original finite support, and each new weight is the sum of the
    43	weights in the corresponding fiber. -/
    44	noncomputable def map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    45	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) : Distribution β where
    46	  support := 𝒟.support.image e
    47	  weight := fun b => ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a
    48	  nonnegative := fun _ => Finset.sum_nonneg fun a _ => 𝒟.nonnegative a
    49	  outsideSupport := fun _ hb =>
    50	    Finset.sum_eq_zero fun a ha =>
    51	      (hb (Finset.mem_image.mpr
    52	        ⟨a, (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).1, (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).2⟩)).elim
    53	
    54	@[simp]
    55	theorem map_support {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    56	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) :
    57	    (𝒟.map e).support = 𝒟.support.image e := rfl
    58	
    59	@[simp]
    60	theorem map_weight {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    61	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) (b : β) :
    62	    (𝒟.map e).weight b =
    63	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a := rfl
    64	
    65	/-- Push-forward preserves total mass. -/
    66	theorem map_totalWeight {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    67	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) :
    68	    (𝒟.map e).totalWeight = 𝒟.totalWeight := by
    69	  simpa [totalWeight, map] using
    70	    (Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to
    71	      (s := 𝒟.support) (t := 𝒟.support.image e) (g := e)
    72	      (fun a ha => Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩) 𝒟.weight)
    73	
    74	/-- A finite weighted sum over a push-forward distribution is the corresponding
    75	weighted sum of the pulled-back family.  This is the `Distribution` analogue of
    76	the finite-sum form of `PMF.map`. -/
    77	theorem map_sum_smul {α β M : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
    78	    [AddCommMonoid M] [Module Error M]
    79	    (𝒟 : Distribution α) (e : α → β) (f : β → M) :
    80	    ∑ b ∈ (𝒟.map e).support, (𝒟.map e).weight b • f b =
    81	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    82	  classical
    83	  calc
    84	    ∑ b ∈ 𝒟.support.image e,
    85	        (∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a) • f b
    86	        = ∑ b ∈ 𝒟.support.image e,
    87	            ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support.filter (fun a => e a = b), 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    88	          refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
    89	          intro b _
    90	          rw [Finset.sum_smul]
    91	          refine Finset.sum_congr rfl ?_
    92	          intro a ha
    93	          exact congrArg (fun x => 𝒟.weight a • f x) (Finset.mem_filter.mp ha).2.symm
    94	    _ = ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a • f (e a) := by
    95	          exact Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to
    96	            (s := 𝒟.support) (t := 𝒟.support.image e) (g := e)
    97	            (fun a ha => Finset.mem_image.mpr ⟨a, ha, rfl⟩)
    98	            (fun a => 𝒟.weight a • f (e a))
    99	
   100	end Distribution
   101	
   102	/-- On a finite ambient type, a summand that vanishes outside a distribution's
   103	explicit support has the same total sum over all ambient values as over that support.
   104	
   105	This is a project-local explicit-support adapter around Mathlib's `Finset.sum_subset`:
   106	Mathlib supplies the finite-sum theorem, while this lemma packages the common shape used
   107	when paper expressions sum over a whole question set but the repository stores a smaller
   108	`Distribution.support`.  It is not intended to replace Mathlib probability theory. -/
   109	theorem Distribution.sum_univ_eq_sum_support {α β : Type*} [Fintype α]
   110	    [AddCommMonoid β] (𝒟 : Distribution α) (f : α → β)
   111	    (hf : ∀ a, a ∉ 𝒟.support → f a = 0) :
   112	    (∑ a : α, f a) = ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, f a := by
   113	  classical
   114	  simpa using
   115	    (Finset.sum_subset (Finset.subset_univ 𝒟.support)
   116	      (fun a _ ha => hf a ha)).symm
   117	
   118	namespace Distribution.IsProbability
   119	
   120	/-- Unpack the equality form of the probability invariant. -/
   121	theorem weight_sum_eq_one {α : Type*}
   122	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   123	    ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a = 1 := by
   124	  simpa [Distribution.IsProbability, Distribution.totalWeight] using h𝒟
   125	
   126	/-- A probability distribution has total weight one over any finite superset
   127	of its explicit support. -/
   128	theorem weight_sum_eq_one_of_subset {α : Type*}
   129	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) {s : Finset α}
   130	    (hsubset : 𝒟.support ⊆ s) :
   131	    ∑ a ∈ s, 𝒟.weight a = 1 := by
   132	  have hsum :
   133	      ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a = ∑ a ∈ s, 𝒟.weight a :=
   134	    Finset.sum_subset hsubset (fun a _ ha => 𝒟.outsideSupport a ha)
   135	  exact hsum ▸ h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one
   136	
   137	/-- On a finite ambient type, a probabilistic `Distribution` has total weight `1` even
   138	when its weights are summed over the whole ambient type.
   139	
   140	This packages the explicit-support bookkeeping in `Distribution` for downstream Lean
   141	statements that follow the paper's notation `𝔼_{x ∼ 𝒟}` over the question set rather
   142	than over a stored support finset. -/
   143	theorem weight_sum_univ_eq_one {α : Type*} [Fintype α]
   144	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   145	    (∑ a : α, 𝒟.weight a) = 1 := by
   146	  simpa using h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one_of_subset (Finset.subset_univ 𝒟.support)
   147	
   148	/-- A probability distribution has total weight at most `1`. -/
   149	theorem weight_sum_le_one {α : Type*}
   150	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) :
   151	    ∑ a ∈ 𝒟.support, 𝒟.weight a ≤ 1 :=
   152	  le_of_eq h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one
   153	
   154	/-- Push-forward preserves the probability invariant. -/
   155	theorem map {α β : Type*} [DecidableEq β]
   156	    {𝒟 : Distribution α} (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) (e : α → β) :
   157	    (𝒟.map e).IsProbability := by
   158	  simpa [Distribution.IsProbability, Distribution.map_totalWeight] using h𝒟
   159	
   160	end Distribution.IsProbability
   161	
   162	namespace Distribution
   163	
   164	/-- The Mathlib probability mass function associated to a project `Distribution`
   165	whose total mass is one.
   166	
   167	The construction sends each nonnegative real weight to `ℝ≥0∞` by
   168	`ENNReal.ofReal`; the hypotheses of `PMF.ofFinset` are exactly the project
   169	probability invariant and the stored zero-off-support condition. -/
   170	noncomputable def toPMF {α : Type*} (𝒟 : Distribution α)
   171	    (h𝒟 : 𝒟.IsProbability) : PMF α :=
   172	  PMF.ofFinset (fun a => ENNReal.ofReal (𝒟.weight a)) 𝒟.support
   173	    (by
   174	      rw [← ENNReal.ofReal_sum_of_nonneg (fun a _ => 𝒟.nonnegative a),
   175	        h𝒟.weight_sum_eq_one]
   176	      simp)
   177	    (by
   178	      intro a ha
   179	      rw [𝒟.outsideSupport a ha]
   180	      simp)

     3	/-!
     4	# Uniform subset estimates
     5	
     6	This file contains estimates for the total variation distance between the
     7	uniform distribution on a finite type and the uniform distribution on a
     8	nonempty finite subset, together with averaging bounds for `[0,1]`-valued
     9	functions.  The uniform-subset total-variation identity is proved by transport
    10	through Mathlib probability mass functions.
    11	-/
    12	
    13	open scoped BigOperators
    14	
    15	namespace MIPStarRE.LDT
    16	
    17	/-- Total variation between the uniform distribution on a finite ambient type and
    18	the uniform distribution on a nonempty finite subset.
    19	
    20	This is the elementary finite identity
    21	`TV(uniform α, uniform s) = 1 - |s| / |α|`.  The proof transports the project
    22	`Distribution` statement to Mathlib's uniform probability mass functions. -/
    23	theorem totalVariationDistance_uniformDistribution_uniformOnFinset_eq
    24	    {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Nonempty α]
    25	    (s : Finset α) (hs : s.Nonempty) :
    26	    totalVariationDistance (uniformDistribution α) (Distribution.uniformOnFinset s) =
    27	      1 - (s.card : Error) / (Fintype.card α : Error) := by
    28	  rw [totalVariationDistance_eq_toPMF_sum]
    29	  change PMF.totalVariationDistance
    30	      ((uniformDistribution α).toPMF (uniformDistribution_isProbability α))
    31	      ((Distribution.uniformOnFinset s).toPMF
    32	        (Distribution.uniformOnFinset_isProbability s hs)) =
    33	    1 - (s.card : Error) / (Fintype.card α : Error)
    34	  rw [uniformDistribution_toPMF, Distribution.uniformOnFinset_toPMF]
    35	  exact PMF.totalVariationDistance_uniformOfFintype_uniformOfFinset_eq s hs
    36	
    37	/-- A `[0,1]`-valued function averaged over a nonempty finite subset is bounded
    38	by its ambient uniform average plus the total variation distance between the
    39	two uniform distributions. -/
    40	theorem avgOver_uniformOnFinset_le_uniformDistribution_add_totalVariationDistance
    41	    {α : Type*} [Fintype α] [DecidableEq α] [Nonempty α]
    42	    (s : Finset α) (hs : s.Nonempty)
    43	    (f : α → Error)
    44	    (hf_nonneg : ∀ a, 0 ≤ f a)
    45	    (hf_le_one : ∀ a, f a ≤ 1) :
    46	    avgOver (Distribution.uniformOnFinset s) f
    47	      ≤ avgOver (uniformDistribution α) f
    48	        + totalVariationDistance (uniformDistribution α) (Distribution.uniformOnFinset s) := by
    49	  exact
    50	    avgOver_le_avgOver_add_totalVariationDistance
    51	      (uniformDistribution α) (Distribution.uniformOnFinset s)
    52	      (uniformDistribution_isProbability α)
    53	      (Distribution.uniformOnFinset_isProbability s hs)
    54	      f hf_nonneg hf_le_one
    55	
    56	end MIPStarRE.LDT

    53	
    54	\subsection{Typed samplers, deciders, and verifiers}
    55	\label{sec:typed-samplers}
    56	
    57	\begin{definition}[Typed conditionally linear functions]
    58	  Let $\type$ be a finite set and $V$ be $\F^n$ for some integer $n \geq 0$.
    59	  A \emph{$\type$-typed family of $\ell$-level conditionally linear functions}
    60	  (implicitly, \emph{on $V$}) is a collection $\{L_\tvar\}_{\tvar \in \type}$
    61	  such that, for each $\tvar \in \type$, $L_\tvar$ is an $\ell$-level
    62	  conditionally linear function on~$V$.
    63	\end{definition}
    64	
    65	\begin{definition}[Graph distribution]
    66	  \label{def:graph-distribution}
    67	  Let $G = (U, E)$ be an undirected graph with vertex set $U$ and edge set~$E$.
    68	  Edges in~$E$ are written as multisets $\{u, v\}$ of two vertices; the case $u
    69	  = v$ represents a self-loop.
    70	  Suppose there are $m$ edges, $k$ of which are self-loops.
    71	  Then the \emph{graph distribution $\mu_G$ of~$G$} is the distribution over
    72	  $U\times U$ such that for every $(u, v)\in U\times U$,
    73	  \begin{equation*}
    74	    \mu_G(u, v) =
    75	    \begin{cases}
    76	      1/(2m-k) & \text{if $\{u, v\} \in E$},\\
    77	      0 & \text{otherwise}.
    78	    \end{cases}
    79	  \end{equation*}
    80	  This is identical to the uniform distribution over pairs $(u, v)\in U\times U$
    81	  such that $\{u, v\} \in E$.
    82	\end{definition}
    83	
    84	\begin{definition}[Typed conditionally linear distributions]
    85	  Let $\type$ be a type set and
    86	  $L=\{L_\lvar\}_{\lvar\in\type},R=\{R_\rvar\}_{\rvar\in\type}$ be $\type$-typed
    87	  families of conditionally linear functions on~$V$.
    88	  Let $G = (\type, E)$ be a graph with vertex set $\type$.

   324	        | .point, .aline, .pointVals u, .alinePolys f =>

   326	        | .dline, .point, .dlinePolys f, .pointVals u =>
   327	            decide (dlinePointCondition P xA xB f u)
   328	        | .point, .dline, .pointVals u, .dlinePolys f =>
   329	            decide (dlinePointCondition P xB xA f u)
   330	        | .aline, .aline, .alinePolys f, .alinePolys g => decide (f = g)
   331	        | .dline, .dline, .dlinePolys f, .dlinePolys g => decide (f = g)

+	The distribution $\mu_G$ is uniform on the set of ordered pairs $(u,v) \in U \times U$ with $\{u,v\} \in E$, and that set is nonempty because $E$ is: an edge $\{u,v\} \in E$ yields the ordered pair $(u,v)$. A uniform distribution on a nonempty finite set has total mass one.

# Mathematical Language Guidelines

MIPStarRE Lean names and documentation should be written for readers comparing
the formalization with the paper and blueprint.

This is a project-local supplement to the Mathlib-derived documentation,
naming, and style guides in the lean-conventions skill's `MATHLIB_doc`,
`MATHLIB_naming`, and `MATHLIB_style` references.

## Scope

These guidelines apply to:

- public Lean declaration names and namespace names;
- module docstrings;
- declaration docstrings;
- documentation-visible section comments;
- explanatory comments that describe the mathematical role of a declaration.
- blueprint prose and formalization-support notes;
- issue titles and issue bodies;
- PR titles and PR descriptions.

## Source of Truth

Use terminology from the following sources, in this order:

1. `references/ldt-paper/`
2. `blueprint/src/chapter/`
3. established local conventions in nearby Lean files

When the paper has a term for the object, use that term. For Section 5, for
example, prefer orthogonalization lemma, truncation function, rounding to
projectors, rank reduction, and completing to measurement.

## Reference Notation And Terminology

The notation and terminology of the original reference are the default for
reader-facing mathematical text.  A reader should be able to compare a Lean
docstring, blueprint paragraph, issue, or PR description with the cited source
without first learning a private vocabulary used by the formalization.

When Lean must use a different name or representation, define the deviation in a
location which future readers can find from the affected statement.  Use the
first applicable location in the following order:

1. the declaration docstring of the public object whose name or representation
   differs from the paper;
2. the module docstring of the defining Lean file, when the deviation concerns a
   family of declarations in that file;
3. the relevant blueprint paragraph, when the notation appears only in the
   blueprint;
4. a report under `docs/reports/` or `docs/paper-gaps/`, when the deviation is a
   larger discrepancy between the paper, blueprint, and Lean.

The explanation should say:

- the notation or term used in the paper;
- the Lean object or name which represents it;
- the mathematical reason for the difference, if there is one;
- the scope in which the replacement should be used.

A PR description may mention the deviation, but it should not be the only place
where future readers can learn it.

Formalization-only auxiliary lemmas should be introduced as such.  Their prose
should name the nearby paper equation, theorem, or construction they support,
rather than presenting the auxiliary name as paper terminology.

## Naming Norm

Names and prose should describe the mathematical object, hypothesis, or
conclusion. They should not encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled.

Avoid presenting words such as `pipeline`, `wrapper`, `package`, `raw`,
`oneShot`, or `liveBlock` as mathematical terminology unless the cited source
uses them with that meaning. Likewise, avoid implementation-local substitutes
such as `projectivization` or `spectral truncation` when the paper gives a
clearer phrase.

This is a general rule for the repository, not only a rule for file splits.
Module names, namespace names, public declarations, theorem fields, docstrings,
blueprint-facing names, issue titles, and spec documents should name the
mathematical layer under discussion, not the local workflow step, paper line
number, or implementation history.

### Concrete examples

The table below illustrates the naming norm with examples patterned on the
codebase and on names seen during review.  Some entries are existing names;
others are proposed names for future refactors.  The "avoid" column lists
process-shaped names that encode the history of how the formalization was
assembled; the "prefer" column lists mathematical names that a reader of the
paper or blueprint would recognize.

| `FinalAssembly`                               | `DiagonalCompletion`                      | Paper Lemma 5.17, constructing a diagonal POVM         |
| `OneShotIneq`                                 | `SelfConsistencyDataProcessing` (or existing module `Preliminaries.SelfConsistency.DataProcessing`)           | Paper's data-processing inequality for self-consistency |
| `PipelineCheck`                               | `ErrorPropagationBound` (proposed)                   | The bound that propagates error through the test       |
